title: Principle_of_rationality
summary:
The principle of rationality was coined by Karl R. Popper in a lecture delivered at Harvard in 1963, later published in his book Myth of Framework. According to Poppers rationality principle, agents act in the most adequate way according to the objective situation. It is an idealized conception of human behavior which he used to drive his model of situational analysis.

These models attribute certain aims and information to the actors, forming the logic of the situation, the result of reconstructing meticulously all circumstances of a historical event. The principle of rationality is the assumption that people are instrumental in trying to reach their goals, and this is what drives the model. Popper believed that this model could be continuously refined to approach the objective truth.

Popper called his principle of rationality nearly empty (a technical term meaning without empirical content) and strictly speaking false, but nonetheless tremendously useful. These remarks earned him criticism because seemingly he had swerved from his famous Logic of Scientific Discovery.

In the context of knowledge-based systems, Newell in 1982 proposed the following principle of rationality: If an agent has knowledge that one of its actions will lead to one of its goals, then the agent will select that action. An important philosophical difference between Newell and Popper is that Newell argued that the knowledge level is real in the sense that it exists in nature and is not made up, allowing him to treat the rationality principle as a way of understanding nature. The principle has broad applications across economics, sociology, political science, and artificial intelligence.
